clue.text: Whiskey drunk by pilots while flying is cause of going astray

indicators.note: things sent flying are scattered in all directions, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: W is Whiskey in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that pilots drinking whisky mid-flight will lose their way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk by' just puts the W among the letters of PILOTS WHILE, and all twelve are then rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: The will-o'-the-wisp is a marsh light said to lure night travellers off the safe path, so it is proverbially what leads people astray.

clue.text: Smell in the air soft part of vegetables each cut for rabbits

indicators.note: cutting each word short means both lose their final letter

parts.note: a waft is a smell carried on the air
the soft edible part of a vegetable or fruit is its flesh

explanation.surface: A cook describing the aroma of vegetable flesh sliced up to feed pet rabbits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbits' looks like the animals being fed but is the definition, a verb: to rabbit on is British slang for chattering.
explanation.definitionFit: To rabbit and to waffle both mean to talk at length without saying much, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Bats circle yard

parts.note: a loop is a circular shape
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' reads as the flying animals circling a garden, but it is an adjective meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats is informal for crazy or eccentric, and loopy is another informal word for the same mild madness.

clue.text: Order, say, Bordeaux to be served up with Scandinavian bread for unfussy consumer

parts.note: the Order of Merit, abbreviated OM

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means brought upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: Bordeaux is an example of French wine, vin
bread is slang for money, and the öre is a small coin of Sweden, Denmark and Norway

explanation.surface: A diner ordering Bordeaux with Scandinavian bread, in the manner of someone who eats anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' looks like food but is slang for money, here a Scandinavian coin; 'say' marks Bordeaux as one example of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnivore eats both plants and meat, so it is a consumer that is not picky about its diet.

clue.text: Over-excited twitchy person bites

indicators.note: a bite takes a chunk out of something, so a run of letters is taken from the words beside it

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A jittery, over-excited person nervously biting their nails.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across the end of 'twitchy' and the start of 'person'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyper is a colloquial clipping of hyperactive, describing someone wound up with excess nervous energy.

clue.text: Snakes try hard to fly in this weather

definitions.text: hard to fly in this weather

parts.note: a path or river that snakes winds
a judge tries or hears a case in court

explanation.surface: Snakes straining to take off in bad weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try hard' looks like one phrase, but 'try' belongs to the wordplay and 'hard' begins the definition; both wordplay words are verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Wind shear is a sudden change in wind speed or direction, a notorious hazard for aircraft taking off or landing.

clue.text: Regularly, beginner eats rolls or other breaded meal

indicators.note: something that rolls over is turned end to end, so the order runs backwards
at regular intervals, so every second letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A novice eating bread rolls or some other bread-based meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls' looks like bread in a list of meals but tells you to turn the letters round. A sarnie is British slang for a sandwich.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandwich is a meal made with slices of bread, so as distinct from rolls it is another bread-based bite.

clue.text: Colourful cast fragments after union announcement?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: brightly coloured bits broken off something, perhaps a plaster cast
setter's reading: small coloured paper pieces thrown over a couple once they are pronounced married

explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union or merger, and 'cast' a mould; read instead as a marriage, and cast as thrown.
explanation.definitionFit: Guests throw small pieces of coloured paper over newly married couples just after the ceremony pronounces them husband and wife.

clue.text: Draconic beast very agitated in the confines of wagon

indicators.note: placed within, so one set of letters sits inside the other
confines are the boundaries, so only the outermost letters are used

parts.note: first and last letters

indicators.note: agitated means stirred up, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dragon-like monster thrashing about inside a caged wagon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draconic' here means dragon-like, not harsh as in draconian laws.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a heraldic two-legged winged dragon, so it is a creature of the dragon family.

clue.text: Disapprove of loud quarrel with sister about work that's rejected

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: F is forte, the musical marking for loud
a row is a noisy argument
a nun is a religious sister

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Disapproving of a noisy family row with a sister about some rejected piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: OP for opus (a musical work) and F for forte are standard abbreviations; the sister's letters wrap around the turned-back work.
explanation.definitionFit: To frown upon something is an idiom for regarding it with disapproval, so the phrase is a synonym.

clue.text: Jumper, I'm surprised, is certainly not tight

parts.note: a roo, short for kangaroo, is a famous jumper
'My!' is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Someone remarking in surprise that a sweater fits loosely.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is a British word for a sweater, which is what the surface wants; here it is an animal that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Something roomy has plenty of space inside, so it is loose and far from being a tight fit.

clue.text: New Yorker's break with partner spanning a year

indicators.note: the partner word stretches across, so it goes round the other letters

parts.note: a lover is a romantic partner

explanation.surface: An American takes a break from work alongside a partner over the course of a year.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'New Yorker's' part of the definition signals the American term: a layover is what Britons usually call a stopover.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage a layover is a stopover or pause in a journey, a break between flights.

clue.text: Sound of bug beginning to seduce females probing flower

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: opening letter

indicators.note: a probe pushes inside something, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: in crosswords a flower is something that flows, a river
F is female, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: An insect buzzing as it lures females into a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' looks like an insect but means a minor illness such as a cold, whose sound is a runny-nosed sniff.
explanation.definitionFit: A sniffle is the repeated sniffing noise of someone with a cold, the typical sound of a mild infection.

clue.text: Tough setter from America returned a clue making crossword's opener good

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: US is the abbreviation for the United States
per means a, as in so much per head or a head

indicators.note: making means turning into, so one letter of clue becomes another
the opener of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of crossword is C

explanation.surface: A demanding American crossword setter sends a clue back to make the puzzle's first entry good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tough setter' reads as a hard compiler, but a setter is anything that sets, here a strong adhesive. 'making crossword's opener good' turns the C of clue into G.
explanation.definitionFit: Superglue is a very strong quick-setting adhesive, so it is a tough thing that sets.

clue.text: Rest of productive people are now struggling to fill pages

indicators.note: filling something puts material inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: pp is the abbreviation for pages

indicators.note: struggling suggests writhing and twisting, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Busy workers are struggling to fill pages with writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' looks like 'the remainder of' the people, but it means a break for sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A power nap is a short daytime sleep taken by busy people to recharge and stay efficient at work.

clue.text: This setter's cracking cryptic clues shine

indicators.note: cracking something open means getting inside it, so one piece enters the other
cryptic means puzzling or obscured, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
the setter speaking of what belongs to them says mine

explanation.surface: A setter boasting that their brilliant cryptic clues sparkle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' looks like praise, British for excellent, but it tells you to break into the scrambled word.
explanation.definitionFit: To luminesce is to give off light without heat, so it is a technical verb for glowing or shining.

clue.text: Floor temperature controlled by heater

indicators.note: something controlled is held in check, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: the sun is the great heater of the Earth
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Underfloor heating with its temperature set by a thermostat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floor' looks like the thing being heated, but it is a verb meaning to knock someone flat or astonish them.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to knock them down or leave them dumbfounded, the same as to stun them.

clue.text: Fish left in lake at the bottom, the deepest part?

parts.note: the bass is a fish
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: A fish lurking in the deepest part of a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on 'deep' as low in pitch rather than far down in water; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: The bassline is the lowest-pitched musical line in a piece, so in sound terms it is the deepest voice.

clue.text: First light attracted missing rook

indicators.note: something missing has gone, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: to be drawn to something is to be attracted by it
R is the chess notation for rook

explanation.surface: At daybreak, something lured a rook that has now gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' sounds like the bird, fitting the dawn scene, but it is the chess piece, abbreviated R.
explanation.definitionFit: Dawn is the moment daylight first appears in the morning, so it is the earliest light of the day.

clue.text: Record kept by tax official

indicators.note: something kept by another is held inside it

parts.note: a duty is a tax on goods
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A tax official keeping records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax official' reads as one phrase, but the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy is a second-in-command appointed to act for a superior, so is a type of official.

clue.text: Marriage almost wrecked? Time to get a drink

indicators.note: wrecked means ruined, so the letters are broken up and rearranged
almost means the last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A marriage nearly on the rocks, so it's time to reach for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last letter of Marriage; 'wrecked' then mixes MARRIAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A margarita is a cocktail of tequila, lime and orange liqueur, served in a salt-rimmed glass.

clue.text: Gold ingot's base checked by luxury goods company's accountant

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: something checked is held back or restrained, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: Dior is a French luxury fashion house

indicators.note: in a down clue the base of a word is its lowest, final letter

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: A fashion house's accountant inspecting a gold bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checked' suggests inspection, fitting an accountant, but it signals that one piece is held inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: An auditor is an accountant who examines a company's financial records to confirm they are accurate.

clue.text: Cloth roughly put on seat that old lady's vacated

parts.note: c is circa, Latin for about or roughly

indicators.note: when someone vacates a place they leave it, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: an ottoman is an upholstered seat without a back
ma is a familiar word for mother, an old lady

explanation.surface: A cloth thrown over a chair that an elderly woman has just got up from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is slang for mother, giving MA. In a down clue, 'put on' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Cotton is a soft woven fabric made from the fibres of the cotton plant, so is a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Nick trimmed modest cut of meat

indicators.note: trimmed means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: pure means chaste, modest in conduct
loin is a cut of meat from an animal's back

explanation.surface: A butcher's description of a lean modest joint, neatly trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name or a notch, but it is British slang for steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To purloin is to steal, and to nick is the informal British word for stealing.

clue.text: Shoot, tackling ace winger

indicators.note: to tackle is to grab hold of, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: a bud is a young shoot on a plant
an ace performer is a star

explanation.surface: A command to a footballer to shoot while tackling the star winger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' looks like a wide player in football; in crosswords it can be anything with wings, here a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A bustard is a large heavy ground bird, and anything with wings can be called a winger in crosswords.

clue.text: Joy tipped one pound and two shillings

indicators.note: tipped over means upended, so in a down clue the letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight
s is the abbreviation for a shilling, an old British coin, doubled here

explanation.surface: Delight at being tipped a pound and two shillings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tipped' suggests a gratuity given; it tells you to upend the first two pieces. The shilling was a pre-decimal British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Bliss is a state of perfect happiness, so is a stronger synonym for joy.

clue.text: A portion of land receding on large island

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: receding means moving back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: a lot is a plot or portion of land
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Part of a large island is disappearing under the rising sea.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the reversed piece above the last.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef or chain of islets enclosing a lagoon, a type of island.

clue.text: When to participate in small amount of alcohol?

definitions.text: When to participate in small amount of alcohol?

indicators.note: participating means being inside the group, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits
as, as in 'as I left', means when

explanation.surface: Someone asking at what point they should join in with a little drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a toast is the moment everyone joins in to sip a little drink together.
explanation.definitionFit: At a toast the company raises glasses and all take a small sip together in someone's honour.

clue.text: Go on jet boarded by international singer

indicators.note: a vehicle boarded by passengers has them inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a spout is a jet of liquid
I is the abbreviation for international
a tit is a small songbird, and a songbird is a singer

explanation.surface: An international star singer boarding a private jet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' looks like an aircraft and 'singer' a pop star; one is a spurt of liquid and the other a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Go on!' and 'spit it out!' are both idioms urging a hesitant speaker to say what they mean.

clue.text: Earn little at work, accepting odds of rise to be astronomically remote

indicators.note: letters at work are busy being rearranged into something new

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the odds of a word are its odd-numbered letters, first, third and so on

parts.note: the first and third letters

explanation.surface: A low-paid worker being told that any pay rise is astronomically unlikely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accepting' only adds the two selected letters to the pile before everything is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Interstellar describes the vast space between stars, so it means lying at an astronomical distance away.
